=== TNMP's Responses and Comments to PFP .pdf ===
                                  PUC PROJECT NO. 58000
 RULEMAKING TO UPDATE                             §       PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 WHOLESALE AND IOU RETAIL                         §
 TRANSMISSION COST RECOVERY                       §                    OF TEXAS
 IN THE ERCOT REGION                              §
    TEXAS-NEW MEXICO POWER COMPANY’S RESPONSES TO COMMISSION
             STAFF’S QUESTIONS AND GENERAL COMMENTS

TO THE HONORABLE PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS:

        Texas-New Mexico Power Company (“TNMP”) respectfully submits these comments to

the Public Utility Commission of Texas (“Commission”) in response to Commission Staff’s

(“Staff”) questions for public comment filed on August 11, 2026, related to Rulemaking to Update

Wholesale and IOU Retail Transmission Cost Recovery in the ERCOT Region. TNMP appreciates

the opportunity to submit these responses and comments, and looks forward to collaborating with

Staff on this project.

                         I.     Response to Commission Staff’s Questions

Question 1: Should the values associated with the large load minimum billing demand

provisions be different for large load customers with different contracted peak demands or

different non coincident (“NCP”) demands?

        TNMP does not recommend establishing different minimum billing demand values based

on a customer’s contracted peak demand or NCP demand. Doing so is likely to add unnecessary

complexity and may result in disparate impacts among different types of large-load customers.

The purpose of this rulemaking is to facilitate the interconnection of large loads while ensuring

that transmission costs are appropriately assigned to the customers driving those costs, rather than

shifted to other customers. A uniform approach to the minimum billing demand provisions would

further that objective while promoting simplicity, transparency, and ease of utility administration.




Project No. 58000                                                                           Page 1
 Question 2: Should the large load minimum billing demand be: (a) fixed for 20 years as

proposed; (b) reduced in phases over a period of 20 years; or (c) extended to a longer time

period?

           TNMP does not currently support a fixed 20-year minimum billing demand requirement

and would welcome additional information regarding the basis for the proposed 20-year time frame

to better respond to the Commission’s proposal. The 20-year period appears arbitrary and raises

administrative, operational, and tariff implementation concerns.

           As drafted, it is unclear how the obligation would apply in the event of a change in facility

ownership or how utilities would effectively track and administer the requirement over multiple

decades. Such 20-year minimum billing demand proposal is inconsistent with certain provisions

of TNMP’s current approved tariff. Specifically, under Section 4.3.6 of TNMP’s tariff, and as set

forth in the Pro-forma Tariff for Retail Delivery Service, 1 service to a new retail customer resets

billing demand and is not based on the premises history. TNMP seeks clarity regarding how a

long-term minimum billing demand obligation would survive a change in customer ownership.

           To the extent the purpose of the large load minimum billing demand is to ensure recovery

of transmission infrastructure costs incurred to serve the customer, TNMP does not believe a 20-

year period is supported by the expected life of the underlying transmission assets, which generally

extend well beyond 20 years. If the Commission determines that a minimum billing demand is

necessary to facilitate cost recovery, the recovery period should be tied to the underlying

infrastructure investment rather than the proposed arbitrary 20-year time frame. TNMP further

notes that administratively managing such obligations over multiple decades, and across potential




1
    16 Texas Administrative code (“TAC”) §25.214 (d) Pro-forma Retail Delivery Tariff.

Project No. 58000                                                                               Page 2
 new retail customers at existing premises, is complex and necessarily requires consideration of

utility systems, pro forma tariff provisions, and customer transitions.

Question 3: Should the large load minimum billing demand be based on some measure of

demand lower than contracted peak demand and NCP demand? For example, should the large

load minimum billing demand: (a) reflect a "ratcheted" demand, wherein the large load

minimum billing demand is some percentage of the customer's contracted peak demand or

maximum NCP demand in the previous year? If so, should the ratchet percentage decline in

phases over the years, and how? Or (b) be based on a "weighted average" minimum billing

demand, wherein the large load minimum billing demand is some weighted average of the large

load customer’s contracted peak demand or highest NCP demand over the previous year and

the large load customer's 12CP demand? If so, should the percentage weighting towards

contracted peak demand or NCP demand decline in phases over the years, and how?

       TNMP supports using a customer’s contracted peak demand as the basis for large load

minimum billing demand and does not support more complicated alternatives such as ratcheted

demand calculations, weighted-average methodologies, or similar mechanisms. TNMP

recommends that simplicity, transparency, and ease of utility administration should be the key

objectives of any minimum billing demand framework.

       Using contracted peak demand appropriately aligns cost responsibility directly to

individual customer service requests. Utilities plan and construct facilities based on specific

capacity requested by a customer, and such investments in infrastructure are made to ensure that

requested (and approved) load can be effectively served. If a customer requests 300 MW of service,

the utility must build and ultimately maintain the infrastructure necessary to accommodate that

load request regardless of whether the customer ultimately utilizes the full amount of capacity. If

the minimum billing demand is set at a level below the customer’s contracted demand, a portion

Project No. 58000                                                                          Page 3
 of the costs incurred to serve that customer may be shifted to other customer classes contradicting

long-standing cost causation principles.

       Accordingly, TNMP believes the minimum billing demand should remain focused on the

customer’s requested service level rather than incorporating ratchets, weighted averages, or other

complex calculations. Such alternatives only increase implementation and administrative

complexity without providing clear corresponding benefits. A straightforward approach based on

contracted peak demand would provide greater certainty for both customers and utilities while

encouraging customers to carefully evaluate and accurately forecast their capacity needs and

subsequent requests. For large load customers, contracted demand should reflect limitations on

available demand resulting from a large load allocation or batch process, ensuring that the

minimum billing demand is based on the capacity actually available to the customer.

Question 4: Should separate rate treatment be applied to a large computational load, defined

as an entity that is subject to §25.194 of this title (relating to Large Load Interconnection

Standards) and in which 50% or greater of the demand at the site consists of power electronic

based load, specifically computational load, such as data centers and cryptocurrency mining

facilities? Responses to this question should include applicable legal support or limitations

regarding separate rate treatment for large computational loads.

       TNMP does not support establishing a separate rate class for large computational loads.

Instead, TNMP believes large computational loads should generally remain within the rate class

that would otherwise apply based on the voltage level. However, TNMP recognizes that some form

of alternative tariff treatment may be appropriate to implement the large load requirements on

computational loads as requested by the legislature and proposed by the Commission.

       Specifically, TNMP recommends consideration of a separate sub-classification applicable

to large computational loads that can sufficiently incorporate additional obligations required under

Project No. 58000                                                                           Page 4
 Commission rules, such as minimum billing demand requirements or additional financial

assurances. This approach would allow large computational loads to remain within the existing

rate design framework based on voltage while recognizing specific mandates associated with large

computational load interconnections. Such proposed treatment would be similar to more recent

Commission-approved tariff structures applicable to primary service substation customers, in

which customers remain within an existing rate framework but are subject to distinct tariff

provisions that reflect their particular service characteristics.

        TNMP notes that the large load interconnection requirements established by the

Commission generally apply based on the characteristics of the load and not solely on customer

size. Accordingly, any differentiated tariff treatment should focus on implementing those specific

requirements rather than establishing a separate rate class or fundamentally altering transmission

rate design. For example, a large computational load could be subject to additional tariff provisions

relating to minimum billing demand requirements, financial security requirements, or other

Commission-directed obligations while continuing to pay the same underlying rates as other

customers taking comparable service at comparable voltage.

        Consistent with Governor Greg Abbott’s June 10 directive to ensure that data centers bear

the costs of the infrastructure required to serve them and that residential customers are not left

subsidizing computational load investments, TNMP recommends that large computational load

customers should be responsible for the costs associated with the transmission infrastructure

constructed to serve their specific load. Accordingly, any Commission-approved mechanism for

the collection and allocation of revenues in excess of transmission costs for this specific sub-

category should be administered solely within the large computational load framework and not

applied more broadly to all large loads.




Project No. 58000                                                                            Page 5
        From a legal perspective, TNMP does not believe this approach would constitute

impermissible discrimination because the differentiated treatment is based on objective

characteristics and regulatory requirements applicable to large computational loads. Texas courts

have recognized that differential treatment is not inherently discriminatory where it is supported

by legitimate distinctions and a reasonable regulatory basis. For example, in City of El Paso v. El

Paso Electric Co., 851 S.W.2d 896 (Tex. App. Austin 1993, writ denied), the court upheld the

Commission’s application of different ratemaking treatment in a fuel-reconciliation proceeding,

recognizing that differing treatment may be appropriate when reasonably supported by the facts

and regulatory objectives at issue. Similarly, a separate tariff schedule or sub-classification for

large computational loads would reflect the unique operational and financial requirements

applicable to those customers while preserving the underlying rate structure applicable to the

broader large load customer class.

       Accordingly, TNMP supports specific tariff treatment for large computational loads

through a sub-classification but does not support creating an entirely new and separate rate class

for such customers.

Question 5: Should the definition for transmission interconnection costs be broadened to

include transmission projects that are recommended at the conclusion of a batch study to serve

the transmission capacity needs of a particular load?

       TNMP does not support broadening the definition of “transmission interconnection costs”

to include transmission projects recommended through a batch study. TNMP requests that the

Commission maintain a clear distinction between customer-specific transmission interconnection

costs and broader transmission system upgrade costs. Specifically, transmission interconnection

costs should be limited to the facilities and costs directly required to interconnect a customer to

the transmission system while transmission projects identified through a batch study may include

Project No. 58000                                                                          Page 6
 broader network upgrades that are more appropriately recovered through traditional rate-based

mechanisms rather than CIAC-type treatment.

        Accordingly, TNMP recommends that the Commission maintain a narrow definition of

transmission interconnection costs and provide additional clarification regarding the distinction

between transmission interconnection costs and broader transmission system upgrades.

Question 6: If a large load customer is able to reserve transmission capacity irrespective of

whether the large load customer has energized or is fully using available capacity, how should

these loads be reflected in the resource adequacy reports and assessments and transmission

planning studies?

        Additional clarification is requested regarding the meaning of “reserve transmission

capacity” for purposes of this question. To the extent the term refers to capacity associated with a

load that has executed an applicable interconnection agreement and has been included in

transmission planning studies, TNMP recommends that load should continue to be reflected in

resource adequacy assessments and transmission planning analyses consistent with the information

utilized during the initial planning process.

        Once a load has been studied and incorporated into transmission planning, utilities evaluate

and develop the infrastructure necessary to serve that requested load. Therefore, such load should

remain reflected in transmission planning and resource adequacy assessments even if the customer

has not yet fully energized or is not yet utilizing its full requested capacity.

        Ultimately, TNMP recommends that any treatment of such large loads should conform

with the Commission’s broader large load interconnection and batch-study framework. Rather than

creating complex methodologies for “reserved transmission capacity,” the Commission should

rely on the existing interconnection, study, and planning processes to determine when and how a




Project No. 58000                                                                           Page 7
 load should be reflected in ongoing or future resource adequacy and transmission planning

assessments.

                     II.    General Comments on Proposed 16 TAC § 25.192

§ 25.192(b)(13) Transmission Interconnection Costs

       TNMP supports clarifying the definition of “Transmission Interconnection Costs” but

recommends revisions to ensure consistency with existing Commission definitions and to clearly

limit the scope of recoverable costs.

       Specifically, the proposed definition references the interconnection of a “transmission-

level customer.” This terminology creates ambiguity when compared to the Commission's existing

definition and use of “transmission service customer” in 16 TAC § 25.5(141). To the extent

stakeholders propose revising the rule to expressly refer to transmission-level retail customers,

such an approach is likely to conflict with the Commission’s existing definition of “transmission

service customer,” which expressly provides that a retail customer, as defined in 16 TAC §

25.5(113) may not be a transmission service customer. Accordingly, the Commission should

clarify that the reference to “transmission-level customer” in the proposed definition for

transmission interconnection costs refers solely to a customer’s physical point of interconnection

and does not alter the customer’s regulatory classification or ultimate status as a retail customer.

       TNMP also recommends expressly excluding broader transmission network upgrades and

system improvements intended to provide regional, reliability, or system-wide benefits.

Transmission interconnection costs should be limited to facilities directly required to physically

interconnect a specific customer to the existing transmission system and should not include broader

network upgrades identified through transmission planning processes.

§ 25.192(f)(1)(B) Billing Units




Project No. 58000                                                                             Page 8
        TNMP has concerns that the proposed methodology requiring ERCOT to adjust

Distribution Service Provider (“DSP”) 12CP billing determinants based on each customer’s

minimum billing demand will be unnecessarily complicated to administer. Additionally, the

burdensomeness of this methodology and proposed timing raises general concerns of practical

implementation for ERCOT, transmission service providers (“TSP”), and DSPs. Under the

proposal, ERCOT would be required to collect and track both actual load and minimum billing

demand information, perform customer-specific adjustments, annualize those adjustments when

service levels change during the year, and incorporate the resulting values into DSP-level billing

determinants used for transmission cost allocation.

       TNMP recommends a more straightforward approach that continues to rely on ERCOT’s

measured 12CP load data for transmission cost allocation purposes while separately billing large

load customers for any difference between their actual load and applicable minimum billing

demand. This approach achieves the Commission’s objective of holding customers accountable

for allotted capacity without requiring modifications to established billing determinant calculations

or transmission cost allocation methodologies. Because ERCOT should already possess the

information necessary to identify contracted load obligations through the interconnection and

study processes, and can track customer load on an ESI ID basis, the incremental charge associated

with unused allotted capacity can be addressed directly via customer billing. This alternative

approach would reduce administrative burden, increase transparency for both customers and

utilities, and more directly distinguish between capacity requested by a large load customer and

capacity actually utilized on an individual utility system.

§ 25.192(j)(6) Interim Update of Network Rates – DSP’s Right to Pass Through Changes in

Wholesale Rates




Project No. 58000                                                                            Page 9
        TNMP opposes deletion of § 25.192(j)(6). This provision expressly recognizes a DSP’s

ability to expeditiously pass through Commission-approved changes in wholesale transmission

rates pursuant to § 25.193. The proposed deletion removes such express authority and may create

unnecessary ambiguity regarding cost recovery of wholesale transmission rate changes. Therefore,

TNMP recommends that this specific language should remain unchanged.

§§ 25.192(k)(1-2) Large Load Customer Interconnection Fee and Financial Security

       TNMP recommends clarifying the treatment of interconnection fees and forfeited financial

security under proposed §§ 25.192(k)(1-2) to ensure consistency with the proposed offset to the

interconnecting TSP’s rate base as in PUC Docket No. 58481. As drafted, this proposal appears

to contemplate reducing the transmission revenue requirement by the amount of interconnection

fees or forfeited financial security. However, these amounts are generally treated as offsets to

capital investment rather than recurring revenue requirement credits.

       Further, TNMP recommends that the rule expressly address amortization and specify the

time period over which any offset will be applied. Without amortization considerations, applying

the full amount as an immediate reduction to the transmission revenue requirement creates timing

concerns that may potentially result in applying the same offset amount more than once. TNMP

recommends that any interconnection fee or forfeited financial security offset be amortized over

five years. A five-year amortization period offers a more gradual and sustainable customer benefit

by spreading direct rate impacts over time, rather than applying an entire offset in a single year,

while also maintaining established ratemaking principles. TNMP therefore recommends revising

§§ 25.192(k)(1-2) to align with the offset framework proposed in Project No. 58481.

§ 25.192(l) Transition Requirements

       TNMP requests clarification and revisions to proposed § 25.192(l) to ensure a consistent

and effective transition from 4CP to 12CP billing demands. While subsection (l)(1) establishes

Project No. 58000                                                                         Page 10
 when the initial 12CP billing demands become effective and subsection (l)(2) requires conforming

tariff revisions, the proposal does not address necessary recalculation of transmission rates. A TSP

cannot simply replace a 4CP billing demand with a 12CP billing demand while continuing to apply

rates developed utilizing 4CP billing determinants. Such an approach could result in significant

under recovery of transmission costs because billing determinants must be developed in

conjunction with transmission rates.

       TNMP further recommends that the Commission clarify the timing of 12CP

implementation. To support the development of appropriate 12CP billing determinants using 30-

minute interval data, TNMP recommends allowing sufficient time for TSPs to update their systems

to calculate billing determinants based on 30-minute intervals. TNMP recommends that the

transition to 12CP billing demands not become effective until sufficient data are available to

develop billing determinants and corresponding transmission rates that accurately reflect customer

behavior under the new 12CP framework. This approach would support a more accurate and

equitable transition while minimizing the risk of cost under recovery and unintended rate impacts.

       Unlike certain other ratemaking mechanisms, recovery of wholesale transmission

investments does not include a true-up process that would sufficiently allow for corrections arising

from any resulting consequences. Therefore, TNMP recommends that any prescribed transition

process expressly allow for recalculation of transmission rates based on the proposed new 12CP

billing determinants. At minimum, the rule should clarify the sequence of steps required for 12CP

implementation, including (1) 12CP approval, (2) tariff revisions, (3) recalculation of rates, and

(4) any required updates to Transmission Cost Recovery Factors (“TCRF”).

       TNMP is also concerned that the 30-day compliance filing requirement in subsection (l)(2)

may not be feasible given the scope of implementation actions required to transition from 4CP to

a 12CP framework. In particular, development of new billing determinants will require the

Project No. 58000                                                                          Page 11
 collection and analysis of significant customer usage data under the new 12CP framework that

cannot reasonably be completed within 30 days of rule adoption. Additionally, the explicit

restriction that a compliance filing “may not include any other changes” may be impractical if the

filing deadline overlaps with other required Commission-directed tariff updates.

       TNMP recommends that the Commission establish a separate compliance project to

address implementation of the proposed 12CP framework. Such a project could include one or

more stakeholder workshops to identify and resolve implementation issues, including concerns

that may not yet be recognized by market participants. Such a compliance proceeding would

provide stakeholders and Commission staff with an opportunity to develop practical

implementation timelines, address necessary tariff and rate design revisions, and ensure that any

transition to 12CP are completed in a consistent and effective manner. At a minimum, TNMP

recommends providing additional time for compliance to allow for the development of new billing

determinants and related rate calculations.

       Finally, TNMP notes that the transition raises broader implementation considerations that

are not addressed in the proposal, including wholesale transmission charge implementation, rebills,

and historical billing corrections that span the transition from 4CP to 12CP billing determinants,

and necessary market transaction changes. For example, implementation of 12CP billing requires

Texas SET modifications to accommodate the new billing methodology. ERCOT would also need

to facilitate retail market testing to implement a Texas SET change to incorporate 12CP billing

determinants on the applicable 810_02 invoice transactions. The scope and complexity of these

changes will depend on the transition and implementation framework ultimately adopted by the

Commission.

       Alternatively, to facilitate an accelerated transition, the Commission could consider a

simplified transition approach under which all applicable customers are billed using a non-

Project No. 58000                                                                         Page 12
 coincident peak (“NCP”) billing determinant rather than maintaining separate 4CP and 12CP

billing methodologies. Such an approach may reduce the need for extensive Texas SET

modifications and facilitate a more efficient transition, although the operational and market

impacts of any alternatives would need to be vetted through a stakeholder workshop process.

          In short, the rule appears to assume that changing the billing determinant from 4CP to 12CP

is merely a terminology change within retail tariffs. However, the proposed change from 4CP to

12CP fundamentally affects the calculation of transmission rates and therefore requires

corresponding rate recalculations and detailed implementation procedures to prevent cost recovery

errors.

                            III.   General Comments on 16 TAC § 25.193

§§ 25.193(b-c) – Distribution Service Provider Transmission Cost Recovery Factor (TCRF)

          TNMP recommends maintaining the current language in §§ 25.193(b) and (c) regarding

transmission service costs utilized to fix base rates and Commission-approved cost changes. As

proposed, the revisions eliminate references to transmission costs embedded in base rates and

modify the existing TCRF calculation methodology in a manner that may be interpreted as limiting

the Commission’s future flexibility to incorporate transmission-related costs into base rates or

otherwise adjust cost recovery mechanisms as circumstances warrant. TNMP does not believe

such a restriction is necessary and recommends preserving the current framework, which provides

the Commission with discretion to determine the appropriate ratemaking treatment of transmission

costs.

          Similarly, TNMP is also concerned with the proposed removal of language authorizing

recovery of “cost changes approved or allowed by the Commission to the extent that such costs

vary from the transmission service cost utilized to fix the base rates of the DSP.” This language

expressly recognizes the Commission’s authority to address changes in transmission-related costs

Project No. 58000                                                                           Page 13
 and provides flexibility to accommodate future ratemaking adjustments. Removing this provision

creates uncertainty regarding the Commission’s ability to allow or approve varied transmission

costs necessary to remedy base rate issues of a DSP.

§ 25.193(d) Large Load Minimum Billing Demand

       TNMP recommends revising § 25.193(d) to address circumstances in which a large load

customer’s contracted capacity exceeds the capacity that is actually available to serve the

customer. As drafted, the provision does not appear to recognize situations in which a customer

has executed an agreement for a specified level of capacity when the utility is only able to make a

portion of that capacity available as transmission system capacity is still being built out. In those

situations, utilizing a minimum billing demand solely on the contracted amount may not accurately

reflect the transmission system capacity available to the customer. TNMP believes the minimum

billing demand should be based on the customer’s full contracted demand commitment, with

consideration of lesser capacity apportioned by ERCOT through a large load allocation or batch

process.

       Additionally, although a customer may ramp up load over time pursuant to an agreed-upon

ramp schedule, the utility must proceed with constructing necessary facilities to satisfy the

customer’s full contracted demand. Accordingly, minimum billing demand should not be reduced

solely because a customer’s actual usage has not yet reached its full contracted level pursuant to a

ramp schedule. This approach is consistent with the purpose of ERCOT capacity allocation under

existing processes, which are designed to ensure that customers bear the costs associated with

planned and allocated capacity for their future needs. If a customer is unwilling to pay the

applicable minimum billing demand or fails to satisfy its ramp schedule commitments, the utility

should then have the ability to reevaluate the customer’s allocated capacity and, where appropriate,

reallocate excess capacity to other customers seeking service.

Project No. 58000                                                                           Page 14
        By way of example, say a customer seeks to connect 700 MW of load, but through

ERCOT’s allocation process receives only 500 MW of allocated capacity, meanwhile only 400

MW of transmission capacity is currently available to serve the customer while additional system

upgrades are being completed. If that same customer only utilizes 300 MW of demand, TNMP

believes the minimum billing demand should nevertheless be based on the 400 MW of capacity

available to serve the customer. In this circumstance, a minimum billing demand based on the full

500 MW allocation would overstate the capacity currently available, while a minimum billing

demand based on the customer’s 300 MW actual usage would fail to recognize the allocated and

planned transmission capacity for the customer’s benefit. Accordingly, TNMP recommends that

the rule clarify that minimum billing demand should reflect the capacity actually available to serve

the customer regardless of their intended ramp schedule usage.

       TNMP further recommends that the Commission clarify how available capacity will be

determined and whether ERCOT will provide or verify the information necessary to support

available capacity calculations. Without a clear and consistent methodology, utilities and

customers may face uncertainty regarding the proper calculation of minimum billing demand

obligations. Accordingly, TNMP believes that minimum billing demand should be based on the

customer’s contracted demand commitment, including any capacity allocated pursuant to a large

load allocation or batch process, rather than actual usage levels or alternative ratcheted

methodologies. Although a customer may increase usage over time in accordance with an agreed-

upon ramp schedule, the utility must proceed with facility construction to serve the customer’s

contracted demand. Accordingly, TNMP recommends revising the rule to clarify that minimum

billing demand calculations should reflect the capacity allocated for the customer and to establish

a clear process for determining the contracted demand value used in those calculations.

§ 25.193(e) Adjustments Due to Delayed Cost Recovery or Billing Information

Project No. 58000                                                                          Page 15
        As discussed in response to Question 4, large computational loads should generally remain

within the otherwise-applicable voltage level-based rate class, while being subject to additional

tariff provisions necessary to implement Commission and legislative directives. Establishing a

sub-classification would provide a transparent mechanism for applying any Commission-approved

adjustments under subsection (e), including adjustments associated with delayed cost recovery,

anticipated billing units, or recoveries attributable to large computational load customers, without

altering the underlying transmission rate design applicable to similarly situated customers taking

service at the same voltage level.

       Consistent with the policy objective that large computational loads bear the costs

associated with the infrastructure constructed to serve those loads and that other customers do not

subsidize such investments, TNMP recommends that any adjustments authorized under subsection

(e) that are specifically attributable to large computational load customers be tracked and allocated

within the applicable large computational load sub-classification. This sub-classification approach

would provide a reasonable framework for the recovery of costs uniquely associated with serving

large computational load customers.

§ 25.193(f) TCRF Charges

       TNMP opposes the removal of language providing authority to Commission orders issued

in rate proceedings. Removal of this language creates ambiguity regarding the treatment of interim

rates approved by Commission order and other Commission-approved rate adjustments that remain

in effect pending a final rate case resolution. Retaining the current language is necessary to ensure

that TCRF charges continue to reflect Commission-approved transmission rates.

§ 25.193(g) Reports

       TNMP recommends removing the reporting requirements detailed in subsection (g)

because the required information is already provided by utilities in their TCRF filings. The data

Project No. 58000                                                                           Page 16
 necessary to determine class-specific cost recovery, including calculations of over and under

recoveries, is submitted as part of a TCRF proceeding and is readily available for Commission

review. Imposing an additional separate reporting requirement is duplicative and increases

administrative burdens on utilities without providing additional regulatory value. At a minimum,

the rule should clarify that information submitted in a TCRF filing satisfies any reporting

obligations under this subsection.

                               IV.     General Comments on §25.252

§ 25.252(c) TSP and IOU-DSP Tariff Requirements

       TNMP recommends that the Commission develop and adopt pro forma large load tariff

language applicable to all TSP and IOU-DSP tariffs. Incorporating large load requirements into

the Commission’s existing pro forma tariff would promote consistent implementation of the

Commission’s large load requirements, reduce potential for unintended application of the rules

among utilities, and offer increased transparency for customers.

       TNMP notes that several of the provisions proposed in this docket overlap with issues

currently being considered in PUC Docket No. 58481 regarding large load interconnection

standards. Given the timing of the concurrent rulemakings, utilities and stakeholders may have

limited opportunity to reconcile overlapping or inconsistent requirements before PUC Docket No.

58481 is finalized. To avoid conflicting obligations and implementation issues, the Commission

should ensure that the requirements adopted in PUC Docket Nos. 58000 and 58481 are aligned.

       Alternatively, TNMP recommends that the Commission evaluate whether certain

requirements, including financial security provisions, should be consolidated within a single

rulemaking to avoid duplication or inconsistencies. Regardless of the approach ultimately adopted,

incorporation of standardized large load provisions into the Commission’s pro forma tariff would

facilitate uniform implementation across all utilities.

Project No. 58000                                                                        Page 17
 §§ 25.252(e)(1-2) Commencement of Billing

       TNMP recommends that the Commission establish a clear, bright-line process for

determining when billing obligations commence under this subsection. Specifically, the rule

should identify (1) when capacity is deemed available to serve the large load customer and (2) the

entity responsible for making that determination. Without a clearly defined process,

implementation could vary among utilities and customers, leading to unnecessary disputes

regarding appropriate billing commencement dates.

       Because ERCOT is uniquely positioned to evaluate system conditions and transmission

availability, TNMP believes that ERCOT is the most appropriate entity to determine when capacity

has become available. Additionally, if billing is triggered based on the availability of capacity, the

rule should expressly authorize utilities to apply charges retroactively starting on the date ERCOT

determined capacity became available. Such authorization is necessary because the determination

may not occur contemporaneously with the date capacity first became available. Without a clear

mechanism to backfill charges, utilities may be prevented from recovering amounts that should

otherwise have been collected starting on the first day of available capacity.

       TNMP also notes potential practical billing challenges associated with the proposed

“greater of” billing requirement. The Commission should ensure that any such “greater of” billing

requirement can be implemented through existing billing systems or otherwise provide sufficient

guidance regarding how such calculations should be performed and communicated. TNMP further

notes that subsection (e)(2)(ii) should recognize that transmission and distribution utilities receive

payment from a customer’s Retail Electric Provider (“REP”), rather than directly from the end-use

retail customer. Revising the language to reflect the REP-based billing structure is most consistent

with current Texas utility operations.




Project No. 58000                                                                            Page 18
        Lastly, TNMP has reviewed the proposed rules with the understanding that they apply to

all large load customers that have the ability to take electric service from the ERCOT grid,

regardless of behind-the-meter, net metering, or other bring your own generation arrangements.

Customers that retain access to grid service as a contingency ultimately benefit from capacity

considerations on their behalf and should bear the costs associated with maintaining that capacity

for their contingency purposes. Otherwise, such costs may be unfairly shifted to other customer

classes. TNMP therefore recommends that the Commission consider minimum billing demand

requirements or a specific standby demand charge for customers that maintain the ability to rely

on grid service.

       TNMP supports the Commission’s objective of ensuring that large load customers pay an

appropriate share of the costs associated with the capacity allotted to serve them. To effectively

achieve that objective, the Commission should adopt clear and administrable minimum billing

demand requirements, provide sufficient time and guidance for implementation of the transition to

12CP billing demands, and establish a compliance project with stakeholder workshops to address

the numerous billing, settlement, Texas SET, ERCOT, and operational concerns implicated by the

proposal. These revisions will promote regulatory certainty, reduce implementation discrepancies,

and help ensure that the costs of serving large load customers are allocated in a fair and cost-

causative manner.




Project No. 58000                                                                        Page 19
        TNMP appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments and looks forward to

continuing to work with the Commission and Staff on these important issues.

Dated: August 11, 2026                             Respectfully submitted,

      EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF TEXAS-NEW MEXICO POWER COMPANY’S
                            COMMENTS

       Texas-New Mexico Power Company (“TNMP”) respectfully submits this executive

summary of its comments to the Public Utility Commission of Texas (“Commission”) in response

to the Commission Staff’s Proposal for Publication to update wholesale and IOU retail

transmission cost recovery in the ERCOT region. TNMP supports the Commission’s objective of

ensuring that transmission costs associated with serving large loads are allocated in a fair and cost-

causative manner. To promote regulatory certainty, administrative efficiency, and consistent

implementation across utilities, TNMP highlights the following high-level recommendations for

Commission review:

       1.      Preserve clear distinctions between customer-specific interconnection costs and

broader transmission system upgrades. Transmission interconnection costs should be limited to

facilities directly required to interconnect a customer to the transmission system and should not

include regional or network upgrades more appropriately recovered through existing transmission

cost recovery mechanisms.

       2.      Adopt a straightforward and administrable approach to minimum billing demand

and transmission cost allocation. The Commission should avoid complex ratchets, weighted-

average calculations, or ERCOT adjustments to DSP billing determinants and instead utilize

approaches that directly assign responsibility for capacity allocated to serve large load customers.




Project No. 58000                                                                            Page 21
        3.      Clarify the treatment of minimum billing demand during phased service

availability. TNMP recommends that minimum billing demand be tied to the transmission capacity

actually available to serve a customer when necessary construction is still being completed, rather

than being based solely on contracted demand, allocated demand, or actual usage. Clear rules

governing available capacity determinations will help ensure equitable cost allocation and

consistent implementation across utilities and customers.

       4.      Retain Commission flexibility and existing authority within the TCRF framework.

TNMP recommends maintaining provisions that recognize transmission costs embedded in base

rates, preserve the Commission’s ability to address future transmission-related cost changes, and

continue to authorize the pass-through of Commission-approved wholesale transmission rate

changes.

       5.      Align treatment of interconnection fees and financial security with Project No.

58481. Any offsets associated with interconnection fees or forfeited financial security should be

treated as offsets to revenue requirement and amortized over an appropriate period rather than

applied as an immediate reduction to transmission revenue requirements.

       6.      Provide sufficient implementation time and establish a structured transition process

for the move from 4CP to 12CP billing determinants. The Commission should allow adequate time

for system modifications, billing determinant development, transmission rate recalculations, Texas

SET changes, ERCOT implementation activities, and associated tariff revisions before requiring

compliance.

       7.      Establish a dedicated compliance proceeding and stakeholder workshop process. A

separate implementation project would allow stakeholders, ERCOT, and Staff to identify and

the transition to 12CP billing determinants.

       8.      Develop standardized pro forma large load tariff provisions and coordinate

implementation across related rulemakings. Uniform tariff language and alignment with PUC

Docket No. 58481 will reduce implementation confusion, improve transparency, and promote

consistent application of large load requirements throughout ERCOT.

                     II.     General Comments on Proposed 16 TAC § 25.192

% 25.192(b)(13) Transmission Interconnection Costs

       TNMP supports clarifying the definition of "Transmission Interconnection Costs" but

recommends revisions to ensure consistency with existing Commission definitions and to clearly

limit the scope of recoverable costs.

        Specifically, the proposed definition references the interconnection of a "transmission-

level customer." This terminology creates ambiguity when compared to the Commission's existing

definition and use of "transmission service customer" in 16 TAC § 25.5(141). To the extent

stakeholders propose revising the rule to expressly refer to transmission - level retail customers ,

such an approach is likely to conflict with the Commission' s existing definition of"transmission

service customer," which expressly provides that a retail customer, as defined in 16 TAC §

25.5(113) may not be a transmission service customer. Accordingly, the Commission should

clarify that the reference to "transmission-level customef' in the proposed definition for

transmission interconnection costs refers solely to a customer' s physical point of interconnection

and does not alter the customer' s regulatory classification or ultimate status as a retail customer.

       TNMP also recommends expressly excluding broader transmission network upgrades and

system improvements intended to provide regional, reliability, or system-wide benefits.

Transmission interconnection costs should be limited to facilities directly required to physically

interconnect a specific customer to the existing transmission system and should not include broader

network upgrades identified through transmission planning processes.

§ 25.192(f)(1)(B) Billing Units

        TNMP has concerns that the proposed methodology requiring ERCOT to adjust

Distribution Service Provider ("DSP") 12CP billing determinants based on each customer' s

minimum billing demand will be unnecessarily complicated to administer. Additionally, the

burdensomeness of this methodology and proposed timing raises general concerns of practical

implementation for ERCOT, transmission service providers ("TSP"), and DSPs. Under the

proposal, ERCOT would be required to collect and track both actual load and minimum billing

demand information, perform customer-specific adjustments, annualize those adjustments when

service levels change during the year, and incorporate the resulting values into DSP-level billing

determinants used for transmission cost allocation.

       TNMP recommends a more straightforward approach that continues to rely on ERCOT' s

measured 12CP load data for transmission cost allocation purposes while separately billing large

load customers for any difference between their actual load and applicable minimum billing

demand. This approach achieves the Commission' s objective of holding customers accountable

for allotted capacity without requiring modifications to established billing determinant calculations

or transmission cost allocation methodologies. Because ERCOT should already possess the

information necessary to identify contracted load obligations through the interconnection and

study processes, and can track customer load on an ESI ID basis, the incremental charge associated

with unused allotted capacity can be addressed directly via customer billing. This alternative

approach would reduce administrative burden, increase transparency for both customers and

utilities, and more directly distinguish between capacity requested by a large load customer and

capacity actually utilized on an individual utility system.

        TNMP opposes deletion of § 25.192(j)(6). This provision expressly recognizes a DSP's

ability to expeditiously pass through Commission-approved changes in wholesale transmission

§§ 25.192(k)(1-2) Large Load Customer Interconnection Fee and Financial Security

       TNMP recommends clarifying the treatment of interconnection fees and forfeited financial

security under proposed §§ 25.192(k)(1-2) to ensure consistency with the proposed offset to the

interconnecting TSP's rate base as in PUC Docket No. 58481. As drafted, this proposal appears

to contemplate reducing the transmission revenue requirement by the amount of interconnection

fees or forfeited financial security. However, these amounts are generally treated as offsets to

capital investment rather than recurring revenue requirement credits.

       Further, TNMP recommends that the rule expressly address amortization and specify the

time period over which any offset will be applied. Without amortization considerations, applying

the full amount as an immediate reduction to the transmission revenue requirement creates timing

concerns that may potentially result in applying the same offset amount more than once. TNMP

recommends that any interconnection fee or forfeited financial security offset be amortized over

five years. A five-year amortization period offers a more gradual and sustainable customer benefit

by spreading direct rate impacts over time, rather than applying an entire offset in a single year,

while also maintaining established ratemaking principles. TNMP therefore recommends revising

§§ 25.192(k)(1-2) to align with the offset framework proposed in Project No. 58481.

% 25.193(d) Large Load Minimum Billing Demand

       TNMP recommends revising § 25.193(d) to address circumstances in which a large load

customer' s contracted capacity exceeds the capacity that is actually available to serve the

customer. As drafted, the provision does not appear to recognize situations in which a customer

has executed an agreement for a specified level of capacity when the utility is only able to make a

portion of that capacity available as transmission system capacity is still being built out. In those

situations, utilizing a minimum billing demand solely on the contracted amount may not accurately

reflect the transmission system capacity available to the customer. TNMP believes the minimum

billing demand should be based on the customer' s full contracted demand commitment, with

consideration of lesser capacity apportioned by ERCOT through a large load allocation or batch

process.
       Additionally, although a customer may ramp up load over time pursuant to an agreed-upon

ramp schedule, the utility must proceed with constructing necessary facilities to satisfy the

customer' s full contracted demand. Accordingly, minimum billing demand should not be reduced

solely because a customer' s actual usage has not yet reached its full contracted level pursuant to a

ramp schedule. This approach is consistent with the purpose of ERCOT capacity allocation under

existing processes, which are designed to ensure that customers bear the costs associated with

planned and allocated capacity for their future needs. If a customer is unwilling to pay the

applicable minimum billing demand or fails to satisfy its ramp schedule commitments, the utility

should then have the ability to reevaluate the customer' s allocated capacity and, where appropriate,

reallocate excess capacity to other customers seeking service.


Project No. 58000                                                                           Page 14
        By way of example, say a customer seeks to connect 700 MW of load, but through

ERCOT's allocation process receives only 500 MW of allocated capacity, meanwhile only 400

MW of transmission capacity is currently available to serve the customer while additional system

upgrades are being completed. If that same customer only utilizes 300 MW of demand, TNMP

believes the minimum billing demand should nevertheless be based on the 400 MW of capacity

available to serve the customer. In this circumstance, a minimum billing demand based on the full

500 MW allocation would overstate the capacity currently available, while a minimum billing

demand based on the customer' s 300 MW actual usage would fail to recognize the allocated and

planned transmission capacity for the customer' s benefit. Accordingly, TNMP recommends that

the rule clarify that minimum billing demand should reflect the capacity actually available to serve
the customer regardless of their intended ramp schedule usage.

       TNMP further recommends that the Commission clarify how available capacity will be

determined and whether ERCOT will provide or verify the information necessary to support

available capacity calculations. Without a clear and consistent methodology, utilities and

customers may face uncertainty regarding the proper calculation of minimum billing demand

obligations. Accordingly, TNMP believes that minimum billing demand should be based on the

customer' s contracted demand commitment, including any capacity allocated pursuant to a large

load allocation or batch process, rather than actual usage levels or alternative ratcheted

methodologies. Although a customer may increase usage over time in accordance with an agreed-

upon ramp schedule, the utility must proceed with facility construction to serve the customer's
contracted demand. Accordingly, TNMP recommends revising the rule to clarify that minimum

billing demand calculations should reflect the capacity allocated for the customer and to establish

a clear process for determining the contracted demand value used in those calculations.

limited opportunity to reconcile overlapping or inconsistent requirements before PUC Docket No.

58481 is finalized. To avoid conflicting obligations and implementation issues, the Commission

should ensure that the requirements adopted in PUC Docket Nos. 58000 and 58481 are aligned.

       Alternatively, TNMP recommends that the Commission evaluate whether certain

requirements, including financial security provisions, should be consolidated within a single

rulemaking to avoid duplication or inconsistencies. Regardless ofthe approach ultimately adopted,

incorporation of standardized large load provisions into the Commission's pro forma tariff would

facilitate uniform implementation across all utilities.

 §§25.252(e)(1-2) Commencement of Billing

       TNMP recommends that the Commission establish a clear, bright-line process for

determining when billing obligations commence under this subsection. Specifically, the rule

should identify (1) when capacity is deemed available to serve the large load customer and (2) the

entity responsible for making that determination. Without a clearly defined process,

implementation could vary among utilities and customers, leading to unnecessary disputes

regarding appropriate billing commencement dates.

       Because ERCOT is uniquely positioned to evaluate system conditions and transmission

availability, TNMP believes that ERCOT is the most appropriate entity to determine when capacity

has become available. Additionally, ifbilling is triggered based on the availability of capacity, the

rule should expressly authorize utilities to apply charges retroactively starting on the date ERCOT

determined capacity became available. Such authorization is necessary because the determination

may not occur contemporaneously with the date capacity first became available. Without a clear

mechanism to backfill charges, utilities may be prevented from recovering amounts that should

otherwise have been collected starting on the first day of available capacity.

       TNMP also notes potential practical billing challenges associated with the proposed

"greater of' billing requirement. The Commission should ensure that any such "greater of' billing

requirement can be implemented through existing billing systems or otherwise provide sufficient

guidance regarding how such calculations should be performed and communicated. TNMP further

notes that subsection (e)(2)(ii) should recognize that transmission and distribution utilities receive

payment from a customer' s Retail Electric Provider ("REP"), rather than directly from the end-use

retail customer. Revising the language to reflect the REP-based billing structure is most consistent

with current Texas utility operations.




Project No. 58000                                                                            Page 18
        Lastly, TNMP has reviewed the proposed rules with the understanding that they apply to

all large load customers that have the ability to take electric service from the ERCOT grid,

regardless of behind-the-meter, net metering, or other bring your own generation arrangements.

Customers that retain access to grid service as a contingency ultimately benefit from capacity

considerations on their behalf and should bear the costs associated with maintaining that capacity

for their contingency purposes. Otherwise, such costs may be unfairly shifted to other customer

classes. TNMP therefore recommends that the Commission consider minimum billing demand

requirements or a specific standby demand charge for customers that maintain the ability to rely

on grid service.

       TNMP supports the Commission' s objective of ensuring that large load customers pay an

appropriate share of the costs associated with the capacity allotted to serve them. To effectively

achieve that objective, the Commission should adopt clear and administrable minimum billing

demand requirements, provide sufficient time and guidance for implementation ofthe transition to

12CP billing demands, and establish a compliance project with stakeholder workshops to address

the numerous billing, settlement, Texas SET, ERCOT, and operational concerns implicated by the

proposal. These revisions will promote regulatory certainty, reduce implementation discrepancies,

and help ensure that the costs of serving large load customers are allocated in a fair and cost-

causative manner.

      EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF TEXAS-NEW MEXICO POWER COMPANY' S

       Texas-New Mexico Power Company ("TNMP") respectfully submits this executive

summary of its comments to the Public Utility Commission of Texas ("Commission") in response

to the Commission Staff' s Proposal for Publication to update wholesale and IOU retail

transmission cost recovery in the ERCOT region. TNMP supports the Commission's objective of

ensuring that transmission costs associated with serving large loads are allocated in a fair and cost-

causative manner. To promote regulatory certainty, administrative efficiency, and consistent

implementation across utilities, TNMP highlights the following high-level recommendations for

Commission review:

        1.     Preserve clear distinctions between customer-specific interconnection costs and

broader transmission system upgrades. Transmission interconnection costs should be limited to

facilities directly required to interconnect a customer to the transmission system and should not

include regional or network upgrades more appropriately recovered through existing transmission

cost recovery mechanisms.

       2.      Adopt a straightforward and administrable approach to minimum billing demand

and transmission cost allocation. The Commission should avoid complex ratchets, weighted-

average calculations, or ERCOT adjustments to DSP billing determinants and instead utilize

approaches that directly assign responsibility for capacity allocated to serve large load customers.




Project No. 58000                                                                            Page 21
        3.      Clarify the treatment of minimum billing demand during phased service

availability. TNMP recommends that minimum billing demand be tied to the transmission capacity

actually available to serve a customer when necessary construction is still being completed, rather

than being based solely on contracted demand, allocated demand, or actual usage. Clear rules

governing available capacity determinations will help ensure equitable cost allocation and

consistent implementation across utilities and customers.

       4.      Retain Commission flexibility and existing authority within the TCRF framework.

TNMP recommends maintaining provisions that recognize transmission costs embedded in base

rates, preserve the Commission' s ability to address future transmission-related cost changes, and

continue to authorize the pass-through of Commission-approved wholesale transmission rate

changes.
       5.      Align treatment of interconnection fees and financial security with Proj ect No.

58481. Any offsets associated with interconnection fees or forfeited financial security should be

treated as offsets to revenue requirement and amortized over an appropriate period rather than

applied as an immediate reduction to transmission revenue requirements.

       6.      Provide sufficient implementation time and establish a structured transition process

for the move from 4CP to 12CP billing determinants. The Commission should allow adequate time

for system modifications, billing determinant development, transmission rate recalculations, Texas

SET changes, ERCOT implementation activities, and associated tariff revisions before requiring

compliance.
       7.      Establish a dedicated compliance proceeding and stakeholder workshop process. A

separate implementation proj ect would allow stakeholders, ERCOT, and Staff to identify and
